why: Atomic structure is the vocabulary of the Chem/Phys section: passages on isotopes, ions, spectra and radioactive tracers all assume you can count particles and read electron configurations quickly.
big: Counting particles: atomic number Z = protons (it names the element); mass number A = protons + neutrons; electrons = Z − charge. Cl⁻ with A = 35 has 17 p, 18 n, 18 e⁻.
Isotopes have the same Z but different neutron counts; they behave the same chemically. Average atomic mass is a weighted average of isotope masses.
Quantum numbers: n (shell, size/energy), ℓ = 0 to n − 1 (s, p, d, f shape), mℓ = −ℓ to +ℓ (orientation), mₛ = ±½. A subshell has 2ℓ + 1 orbitals; a shell holds 2n² electrons.

Filling rules: Aufbau (lowest energy first, n + ℓ rule), Pauli (two electrons per orbital, opposite spins), Hund (fill each orbital singly before pairing). Cr and Cu are exceptions: [Ar]4s¹3d⁵ and [Ar]4s¹3d¹⁰.
Photons and energy levels: E = hf = hc/λ. An electron absorbs a photon to jump up and emits one when it falls; bigger jumps mean higher frequency and shorter wavelength.
Paramagnetic species have unpaired electrons and are drawn into a magnetic field; diamagnetic species have all electrons paired.

ex.q: What is the ground-state electron configuration of Fe²⁺ (Fe, Z = 26), and how many unpaired electrons does it have? (A) [Ar]4s²3d⁴, 4 (B) [Ar]3d⁶, 4 (C) [Ar]3d⁶, 0 (D) [Ar]4s²3d⁴, 2
steps: Neutral Fe has 26 electrons: [Ar]4s²3d⁶.
Transition metals lose their highest-n electrons first, so the two 4s electrons leave: Fe²⁺ = [Ar]3d⁶.
Hund's rule: five d orbitals get one electron each, and the sixth pairs up, leaving 4 unpaired. Answer (B).

trap: Students remove d electrons first when forming transition-metal cations. Fill 4s before 3d, but empty 4s before 3d.
memory: First in, first out: for transition-metal ions, 4s fills first and empties first.

why: Periodic trends let you predict size, ionization energy and electronegativity without memorizing data, and they appear across Chem/Phys passages on bonding, ions, and reactivity.
big: Effective nuclear charge (Zeff) is the pull the valence electrons actually feel: roughly protons minus inner (core) electrons. It rises left to right across a period and drives most trends.
Atomic radius shrinks left to right (higher Zeff, same shell) and grows down a group (new shells). Cations are smaller than their atoms; anions are larger.

Ionization energy (energy to remove an electron) rises left to right and falls down a group, the opposite of radius. Removing a core electron after the valence shell is empty causes a huge jump (e.g., Mg's third IE).
Exceptions: IE dips from group 2 to 13 (Be > B; the p electron is higher in energy) and from group 15 to 16 (N > O; O's paired p electron feels extra repulsion).
Electronegativity rises toward the upper right; F is the most electronegative element (Pauling 4.0). Noble gases are usually left out of electronegativity tables.

Electron affinity generally becomes more favorable (more energy released) toward the upper right, with halogens the most eager to gain an electron (chlorine releases slightly more energy than fluorine, because fluorine's small 2p shell is crowded).

ex.q: Which element has the greater first ionization energy, nitrogen or oxygen, and why? (A) O, because it has more protons (B) O, because it is smaller (C) N, because O loses an electron from a doubly occupied 2p orbital (D) N, because N has a full valence shell
steps: The general trend predicts O > N, since O is to the right. Check for an exception.
N is 2p³ (one electron in each p orbital). O is 2p⁴, so one 2p orbital holds a pair.
The paired electron in O is repelled by its partner and is easier to remove, so O's IE is lower than N's.
Answer: (C).

trap: Students mix up the direction of radius and ionization energy. Remember they run opposite: small atoms hold their electrons tightly, so the smallest atoms have the highest IE.
memory: IE, electronegativity and electron affinity all grow toward the upper right (helium tops IE, fluorine tops electronegativity, chlorine edges out fluorine for electron affinity); only size grows the other way, toward francium.

why: Bonding and intermolecular forces explain boiling points, solubility and molecular shape, so they show up in Chem/Phys passages on drugs, solvents and biomolecules, and again in biochemistry (protein folding, membranes).
big: Ionic vs covalent: a large electronegativity difference (roughly above 1.7) gives ionic bonds, as in NaCl; atoms that share electrons form covalent bonds, which are polar when the electronegativities differ.

Lewis structures and VSEPR: count valence electrons, satisfy octets, then count electron domains around the central atom: 2 → linear (180°), 3 → trigonal planar (120°), 4 → tetrahedral (109.5°). Lone pairs squeeze bond angles (H₂O ≈ 104.5°).
Formal charge = valence electrons − nonbonding electrons − ½(bonding electrons). The best structure has formal charges closest to zero, with any negative charge on the more electronegative atom.
Intermolecular force ranking: ion–dipole > hydrogen bonding > dipole–dipole > London dispersion. Hydrogen bonds need H bonded to N, O or F.
London dispersion exists in every molecule and grows with size and surface area. Long, unbranched chains boil higher than branched isomers of the same formula.
Stronger attractions give a higher boiling point, higher viscosity, higher surface tension and lower vapor pressure. 'Like dissolves like': polar solvents dissolve polar and ionic solutes.

ex.q: Rank from lowest to highest boiling point: neopentane (C(CH₃)₄, 72 g/mol), n-pentane (CH₃(CH₂)₃CH₃, 72 g/mol), 1-butanol (CH₃(CH₂)₃OH, 74 g/mol). (A) n-pentane < neopentane < 1-butanol (B) neopentane < n-pentane < 1-butanol (C) 1-butanol < neopentane < n-pentane (D) neopentane < 1-butanol < n-pentane
steps: The molar masses are nearly equal, so mass does not decide this. Compare the types of attraction instead.
Only 1-butanol has an O–H group, so it can hydrogen bond and boils highest.
The two pentanes have only dispersion forces. Branched neopentane is compact and has less surface contact, so it boils lower than straight-chain n-pentane.
Answer: (B) neopentane < n-pentane < 1-butanol.

trap: Students confuse breaking intermolecular forces (boiling) with breaking covalent bonds. Boiling water separates H₂O molecules and leaves every O–H bond intact. Also, a molecule that contains H and O can hydrogen bond only if the H is attached directly to the O (or to N or F).
memory: Hydrogen bonds need H to be 'FON' (bonded to F, O or N).

why: Mole conversions sit under almost every calculation in the Chemical and Physical Foundations section, from lab-procedure passages to questions on yields, solutions and gas reactions.
big: A mole is 6.02 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number). Particles = moles × 6.02 × 10²³.
Molar mass (g/mol) is the sum of atomic masses in the formula. Moles = mass ÷ molar mass.
The coefficients of a balanced equation are mole ratios, not mass ratios. Always convert grams to moles before using them.
The limiting reactant runs out first and sets the amount of product. Divide each reactant's moles by its coefficient; the smallest result limits.
Percent yield = (actual ÷ theoretical) × 100%. Theoretical yield comes from the limiting reactant.
Percent composition and empirical formula: convert mass percents to moles (assume 100 g), then divide by the smallest number of moles.

ex.q: For N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃, a chemist mixes 28 g N₂ (28 g/mol) with 4.0 g H₂ (2.0 g/mol). What mass of NH₃ (17 g/mol) can form at most? (A) 11 g (B) 23 g (C) 34 g (D) 68 g
steps: Convert to moles: N₂ = 28 ÷ 28 = 1.0 mol; H₂ = 4.0 ÷ 2.0 = 2.0 mol.
Divide by coefficients: N₂ 1.0 ÷ 1 = 1.0; H₂ 2.0 ÷ 3 ≈ 0.67. H₂ is the smaller, so H₂ limits.
NH₃ = 2.0 mol H₂ × (2 NH₃ / 3 H₂) = 4/3 ≈ 1.33 mol.
Mass = 1.33 × 17 ≈ 22.7 g, so the answer is (B) 23 g.

trap: Students compare raw moles (or grams) to find the limiting reactant and forget the coefficients. Divide each reactant's moles by its coefficient first; choice (C) above is the trap answer from assuming N₂ limits.
memory: Grams never go straight to grams: always pass through moles (grams → moles → mole ratio → moles → grams).

why: Kinetics appears in Chemical and Physical Foundations passages that give initial-rate tables, energy diagrams or proposed mechanisms, and it returns in Bio/Biochem as the basis for enzyme catalysis.
big: Rate law: rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ. The orders m and n come from experimental data, not from the coefficients of the balanced equation (unless the step is elementary).

Finding order: change one concentration and watch the rate. Doubling [A] leaves the rate unchanged (zero order), doubles it (first order) or quadruples it (second order); in general the rate changes by 2ᵐ.
Units of k depend on the overall order n: M¹⁻ⁿ s⁻¹. Zero order M s⁻¹, first order s⁻¹, second order M⁻¹ s⁻¹.
Activation energy (Ea) sets the speed: k = A·e^(−Ea/RT). A higher temperature or a lower Ea gives a larger k. Kinetics (Ea) says how fast; thermodynamics (ΔG) says whether.

Catalysts lower Ea for the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster, but ΔH, ΔG and K do not change. A catalyst is used and then regenerated; an intermediate is made and then used up.

Rate-determining step: the slowest step of a mechanism sets the overall rate. The rate law follows from that step's molecularity, but if it contains an intermediate, rewrite the intermediate in terms of reactants from the fast earlier steps.

ex.q: Initial rates for A + B → C: Trial 1, [A] = 0.10 M, [B] = 0.10 M, rate = 2.0 × 10⁻³ M/s. Trial 2, [A] = 0.20 M, [B] = 0.10 M, rate = 4.0 × 10⁻³ M/s. Trial 3, [A] = 0.10 M, [B] = 0.30 M, rate = 1.8 × 10⁻² M/s. What is the rate law? (A) rate = k[A][B] (B) rate = k[A]²[B] (C) rate = k[A][B]² (D) rate = k[B]²
steps: Trials 1 and 2: [A] doubles, [B] is constant, rate doubles (2.0 → 4.0). So the reaction is first order in A.
Trials 1 and 3: [B] triples, [A] is constant, rate rises ninefold (2.0 × 10⁻³ → 18 × 10⁻³). 3ⁿ = 9, so it is second order in B.
Rate = k[A][B]² (third order overall; k = 2.0 × 10⁻³ ÷ (0.10 × 0.010) = 2.0 M⁻² s⁻¹). Answer: (C).

trap: Students read reaction orders straight from the balanced equation. Unless the passage says the step is elementary, find the orders from the data, one reactant at a time.
memory: A catalyst changes the speed, never the destination: same ΔG, same K.

why: Equilibrium sits under acid–base, solubility and oxygen-binding questions, so it appears in Chem/Phys passages on reactions, buffers and blood chemistry.
big: Dynamic equilibrium: forward and reverse reactions keep running at equal rates, so concentrations stay constant but are not necessarily equal.
Equilibrium constant: for aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, K = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b). Leave out pure solids and liquids.
Reaction quotient Q uses the same formula with current amounts. Q smaller than K: shifts right. Q larger than K: shifts left. Q = K: at equilibrium.

Le Châtelier's principle: a system shifts to relieve a stress. Adding reactant or removing product shifts right. For gases, compressing the container (raising pressure) shifts toward the side with fewer moles of gas; adding an inert gas at constant volume causes no shift.
Only temperature changes K. For an exothermic reaction, heating lowers K; for an endothermic one, heating raises K. Catalysts change neither K nor the position.
Link to free energy: ΔG° = −RT ln K, so K greater than 1 means ΔG° is negative (products favored).

ex.q: For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2 NO₂(g), Kc = 0.10 at a certain temperature. A flask holds 0.10 M N₂O₄ and 0.20 M NO₂. What happens? (A) It is at equilibrium (B) It shifts right, making more NO₂ (C) It shifts left, making more N₂O₄ (D) K increases until it equals Q
steps: Write Q = [NO₂]² / [N₂O₄] = (0.20)² / 0.10.
Q = 0.40 is larger than K = 0.10, so there is too much product and the reaction runs in reverse.
Answer: (C). K stays fixed because temperature did not change.

trap: Students think adding a reactant or changing pressure changes K. It only changes Q; the system shifts until Q matches the same K. Only a temperature change moves K itself.
memory: Q small, go right; Q big, go left. K only listens to temperature.

why: Thermochemistry shows up in Chem/Phys passages on combustion, metabolism and phase changes, and the same ΔG logic returns in Bio/Biochem passages on ATP and coupled reactions.
big: Enthalpy (ΔH) is the heat exchanged at constant pressure: ΔH < 0 is exothermic (heat released), ΔH > 0 is endothermic (heat absorbed). Breaking bonds always costs energy; forming bonds releases it, so ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).
Hess's law: ΔH is a state function, so you can add steps. ΔH°rxn = ΣΔH°f(products) − ΣΔH°f(reactants), and ΔH°f = 0 for an element in its standard state (O₂(g), C(graphite)).

Entropy (ΔS) measures how spread out energy and matter are. It rises when moles of gas increase and when solids melt or liquids boil, and it usually rises when a solid dissolves (dissolving small, highly charged ions can lower it, because water molecules become ordered around them). At a phase change, ΔS = ΔH/T.
Gibbs free energy: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, and ΔG < 0 means spontaneous. (−,+) always spontaneous; (+,−) never; (−,−) only at low T; (+,+) only at high T. The crossover is at T = ΔH/ΔS.
ΔG° and K: ΔG° = −RT ln K, so K > 1 means ΔG° < 0. ΔG tells you direction, not speed; a spontaneous reaction can still be very slow.
Calorimetry: q = mcΔT for heating, q = n·ΔH for a phase change (no temperature change during it). Water's c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹, which is high, so water's temperature changes slowly.

ex.q: A reaction has ΔH = +40 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +100 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Above what temperature is it spontaneous? (A) 0.4 K (B) 40 K (C) 400 K (D) It is never spontaneous
steps: Both signs are positive, so the −TΔS term must outweigh ΔH: the reaction becomes spontaneous only at high T.
Convert units so they match: ΔS = 100 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ = 0.100 kJ mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Set ΔG = 0: T = ΔH/ΔS = 40 / 0.100 = 400 K. Above 400 K, ΔG < 0. Answer: (C).

trap: Mixing kJ (for ΔH) with J (for ΔS) gives answers off by a factor of 1000; convert ΔS to kJ before plugging into ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. Also, do not confuse "spontaneous" with "fast."
memory: Bonds: break = take (energy in), make = release (energy out).

why: Gas laws show up in Chem/Phys passages on breathing, scuba diving, blood gases and lab reactions that make or use gases, usually as quick proportional reasoning.
big: Ideal gas law: PV = nRT, with R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) or 8.314 J/(mol·K). Temperature must be in kelvin (K = °C + 273).
Combined gas law: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ when moles are fixed. Boyle (P ∝ 1/V), Charles (V ∝ T) and Avogadro (V ∝ n) are special cases.
STP is 0 °C (273 K) and 1 atm; one mole of ideal gas then fills about 22.4 L.
Dalton's law: P_total = P₁ + P₂ + …, and each partial pressure is Pᵢ = Xᵢ·P_total, where Xᵢ is the mole fraction.
Kinetic molecular theory: average kinetic energy depends only on T (KE = (3/2)kT). Lighter gases move faster: speed ∝ √(T/M), and Graham's law gives rate₁/rate₂ = √(M₂/M₁).
Real gases deviate from ideal behavior at high pressure and low temperature, when molecular volume and attractions matter (van der Waals equation).

ex.q: A 4.0 L balloon at 27 °C and 1.0 atm is warmed to 127 °C while the outside pressure rises to 2.0 atm. About what is its new volume? (A) 1.5 L (B) 2.7 L (C) 5.3 L (D) 9.4 L
steps: Convert to kelvin: 27 °C = 300 K and 127 °C = 400 K.
Use the combined gas law: V₂ = V₁ × (P₁/P₂) × (T₂/T₁) = 4.0 × (1.0/2.0) × (400/300).

trap: Plugging Celsius into a gas law gives nonsense (doubling 20 °C to 40 °C does not double the volume). Convert every temperature to kelvin before you set up a ratio.
memory: Gas laws speak only kelvin: P and V trade places (inverse), V and T move together (direct).

why: Solutions questions show up in Chem/Phys and Bio/Biochem passages about IV fluids, osmosis, lab dilutions and precipitation, where you must handle concentration units and colligative effects without a calculator.
big: Concentration units: molarity M = mol solute / L solution; molality m = mol solute / kg solvent; mass percent = (g solute / g solution) × 100; mole fraction X = mol part / mol total.
Dilution: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂. Adding solvent lowers concentration but keeps moles of solute the same.

Colligative properties depend on the number of dissolved particles, not their identity: ΔT_f = i·K_f·m, ΔT_b = i·K_b·m, osmotic pressure Π = iMRT, and vapor pressure drops (Raoult's law, P = X_solvent·P°).
van't Hoff factor i is the particles per formula unit: glucose 1, NaCl 2, CaCl₂ 3 (ideal).
Solubility and K_sp: for AB₂ ⇌ A²⁺ + 2B⁻, K_sp = [A²⁺][B⁻]². If Q > K_sp a precipitate forms. A common ion lowers solubility (Le Châtelier).
Like dissolves like: polar and ionic solutes dissolve in polar solvents; nonpolar in nonpolar. Gas solubility rises with pressure (Henry's law) and falls with temperature.

ex.q: 5.85 g of NaCl (58.5 g/mol) is dissolved in 0.500 kg of water. Assuming ideal behavior and K_b = 0.51 °C·kg/mol, what is the boiling point of the solution? (A) 100.10 °C (B) 100.20 °C (C) 100.41 °C (D) 101.02 °C
steps: NaCl splits into Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so i = 2.
ΔT_b = i·K_b·m = 2 × 0.51 × 0.200 ≈ 0.20 °C, so the solution boils at about 100.20 °C. Answer (B).

trap: Forgetting the van't Hoff factor, or using molarity where the formula calls for molality. Always count particles first and check whether the denominator is kg of solvent or L of solution.
memory: Colligative = count the particles: more particles, lower freezing point, higher boiling point, bigger osmotic pressure.

why: Acid-base chemistry runs through Chem/Phys and Bio/Biochem passages on buffers, blood pH, titrations, and amino acid charge.
big: Brønsted-Lowry: an acid donates H⁺ and a base accepts it; each acid has a conjugate base. The stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base. A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair.
pH = −log[H⁺], and at 25 °C pH + pOH = 14 and Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴. For a strong acid, [H⁺] equals the acid concentration.
Weak acids ionize partly: Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]. If x is small, [H⁺] ≈ √(Ka·C). Ka × Kb = Kw for a conjugate pair, and pKa = −log Ka.
Buffers pair a weak acid with its conjugate base and resist pH change best near pH = pKa. Use pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).
Titrations: at the half-equivalence point, pH = pKa. The equivalence point is pH 7 for strong acid + strong base, above 7 for weak acid + strong base, below 7 for weak base + strong acid.
Blood is buffered mainly by CO₂/H₂CO₃/HCO₃⁻ near pH 7.4.

ex.q: What is the pH of a 0.10 M solution of a weak acid HA with Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵? (A) 1 (B) 3 (C) 5 (D) 6
steps: Set up Ka = x²/(0.10 − x). Assume x is small: x² ≈ (1.0 × 10⁻⁵)(0.10) = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶.
x = [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ M. Check: 10⁻³ is 1% of 0.10, so the assumption holds.
pH = −log(10⁻³) = 3. Answer: (B).

trap: Students treat a weak acid as if it fully dissociates (giving pH 1 here). Only strong acids (HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄, HClO₄) give [H⁺] = concentration; for weak acids use Ka.
memory: Buffer rule of thumb: each factor of 10 in [A⁻]/[HA] moves pH one unit away from pKa; more base, higher pH.

why: Redox underlies electrochemistry, metabolism (NADH, FADH₂, the electron transport chain) and corrosion, so Chem/Phys and Bio/Biochem passages ask you to assign oxidation states and say which species gains or loses electrons.
big: Oxidation is loss of electrons, so the oxidation number goes up. Reduction is gain of electrons, so the oxidation number goes down. The two always happen together.
Oxidizing agent: the species that is reduced (it takes electrons). Reducing agent: the species that is oxidized (it gives electrons).

Oxidation-number rules: elements alone = 0; monatomic ions = their charge; F = −1; O usually −2 (−1 in peroxides); H usually +1 (−1 in metal hydrides like NaH); group 1 = +1, group 2 = +2; the numbers add up to the overall charge.

Balancing in acid: split into half-reactions, balance atoms other than O and H, add H₂O for O, add H⁺ for H, add e⁻ for charge, then multiply so electrons lost = electrons gained. In base, finish by adding OH⁻ to cancel H⁺.
Organic and biological redox: gaining bonds to O or losing bonds to H is oxidation (ethanol → acetaldehyde). NAD⁺ + 2e⁻ + H⁺ → NADH is a reduction.

ex.q: In acid, dichromate oxidizes iron(II): Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6 Fe²⁺ + 14 H⁺ → 2 Cr³⁺ + 6 Fe³⁺ + 7 H₂O. What is the oxidation number of Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻, and how many electrons does one dichromate ion gain? (A) +6, 6 e⁻ (B) +7, 3 e⁻ (C) +6, 3 e⁻ (D) +12, 6 e⁻
steps: Set the sum equal to the charge: 2x + 7(−2) = −2, so 2x = 12 and x = +6.
Each Cr goes from +6 to +3, gaining 3 e⁻. There are 2 Cr per dichromate, so it gains 6 e⁻.
Check: 6 Fe²⁺ each lose 1 e⁻, which gives 6 e⁻ lost. Electrons lost = electrons gained.
Answer: (A) +6, 6 e⁻. Dichromate is the oxidizing agent.

trap: Students mix up 'oxidized' with 'oxidizing agent.' The species that is oxidized is the reducing agent, and the other way round. Name what happens to the species first, then give the agent the opposite label.
memory: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

why: Electrochemistry shows up in Chemical and Physical Foundations passages on batteries, electroplating, corrosion and nerve or sensor potentials, often linked to ΔG and equilibrium.
big: Anode = oxidation, cathode = reduction, in every cell. Electrons flow through the wire from anode to cathode.
Galvanic cells are spontaneous (E°cell > 0, ΔG° < 0) and their cathode is labeled +. Electrolytic cells need an outside power source, and their cathode is labeled −.
E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode, using standard reduction potentials. Do not multiply E° by coefficients; it is an intensive property.
ΔG° = −nFE°cell, with F ≈ 96,500 C per mole of electrons. Positive E° means negative ΔG° and K > 1.
Electrolysis: charge q = I × t, and moles of electrons = q ÷ F. Use the half-reaction to convert electrons to moles of metal.
The salt bridge lets ions move to keep each half-cell neutral; without it current stops. The Nernst equation, E = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q at 25 °C, gives E away from standard conditions.

ex.q: A current of 2.0 A runs for 965 s through a Cu²⁺ solution, plating copper (63.5 g/mol) on the cathode. About what mass of Cu forms? (F ≈ 96,500 C/mol) (A) 0.32 g (B) 0.64 g (C) 1.3 g (D) 6.4 g
steps: Moles of electrons = 1930 ÷ 96,500 = 0.020 mol e⁻.
Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so moles Cu = 0.020 ÷ 2 = 0.010 mol.
Mass = 0.010 × 63.5 ≈ 0.64 g, so the answer is (B).

trap: Students memorize 'cathode is positive' and apply it to electrolytic cells, where the cathode is negative. Identify electrodes by what happens there (reduction at the cathode), not by the sign.
memory: AN OX and a RED CAT: anode oxidation, reduction cathode, in every cell type.

why: Passages in Chem/Phys and Bio/Biochem name reactants and products by IUPAC or common names, so you must turn a name into a structure quickly before you can answer any reaction question.
big: Parent chain: the longest carbon chain that contains the highest-priority functional group. Roots: meth (1), eth (2), prop (3), but (4), pent (5), hex (6), hept (7), oct (8).
Priority (high → low): carboxylic acid > anhydride > ester > acid halide > amide > nitrile > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine. Halogens and alkyl groups are only ever prefixes.
Numbering: give the highest-priority group the lowest number first, then double or triple bonds, then substituents. List substituents alphabetically, ignoring di-, tri- and tert-.

Suffixes and prefixes: -oic acid, -oate, -amide, -nitrile, -al, -one, -ol, -amine. When a group is not the boss it becomes a prefix: oxo-, hydroxy-, amino-. Aldehyde and acid carbons are C1, so they need no number.
Esters: the alcohol part is named first as an alkyl group, then the acid part with -oate. CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ is ethyl ethanoate (ethyl acetate).
Common names to memorize: formaldehyde (methanal), acetaldehyde (ethanal), acetone (propanone), acetic acid (ethanoic acid), formic acid (methanoic acid), isopropyl alcohol (propan-2-ol).

ex.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂C(=O)CH₃? (A) 2-methylpentan-4-one (B) 4-methylpentan-2-one (C) 4-methylpentanal (D) 2-methylpentan-2-one
steps: The boss group is a ketone (C=O inside the chain), so the suffix is -one. The longest chain through it has 5 carbons: pentan-…-one.
Number so the C=O gets the lowest number. From the right end the C=O is C2; from the left it would be C4. Use the right end.
With that numbering the methyl branch sits on C4. Name: 4-methylpentan-2-one. Answer: (B).

trap: A common error is numbering to give the methyl or halogen the lowest number, which yields names like (A). Always place the suffix group first, then number.
memory: Boss first: find the suffix group, give it the lowest number, then alphabetize the rest.

why: Stereochemistry decides how drugs, sugars and amino acids fit their targets, so it shows up in Chem/Phys and Bio/Biochem passages on reactions and biomolecules.
big: Constitutional isomers share a formula but differ in connectivity (butanal vs butan-2-one). Stereoisomers share connectivity but differ in 3D arrangement.
Chiral center: usually a carbon with four different groups. Rank groups by atomic number (Cahn–Ingold–Prelog), point the lowest away, and read 1→2→3: clockwise = R, counterclockwise = S.
Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images: same physical properties except they rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions. A 50:50 mix (racemic) shows no rotation.
Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images (including cis/trans isomers); they have different physical properties and can be separated by ordinary methods.
Meso compounds have chiral centers but an internal mirror plane, so they are achiral. Maximum stereoisomers = 2ⁿ for n chiral centers, fewer if a meso form exists.
R/S vs (+)/(−): R/S comes from naming rules; the sign of rotation must be measured. One does not predict the other.

ex.q: How many stereoisomers exist for 2,3-dibromobutane, CH₃CHBrCHBrCH₃? (A) 2 (B) 3 (C) 4 (D) 8
steps: C2 and C3 each carry H, Br, CH₃ and the rest of the chain, so there are 2 chiral centers and at most 2² = 4 stereoisomers.
The two halves of the molecule are identical, so the (2R,3S) form has an internal mirror plane: it is meso and the same as (2S,3R).
That leaves (2R,3R), (2S,3S) and one meso form. Answer: (B) 3.

trap: Students apply 2ⁿ without checking for symmetry. Whenever the two ends of a molecule match, look for a meso form and subtract the duplicate.
memory: Mirror image = enantiomer; not a mirror image = diastereomer; mirror plane inside = meso.

why: Hybridization and bond types explain molecular shape, bond strength and reactivity, so they sit underneath almost every organic question in the Chem/Phys section and many biomolecule passages.
big: Steric number (σ bonds + lone pairs on an atom) sets hybridization: 4 → sp³, tetrahedral, 109.5°; 3 → sp², trigonal planar, 120°; 2 → sp, linear, 180°.
σ and π bonds: a single bond is 1 σ; a double bond is 1 σ + 1 π; a triple bond is 1 σ + 2 π. σ bonds come from head-on overlap; π bonds come from side-by-side overlap of unhybridized p orbitals.
Restricted rotation: twisting a double bond would break the π overlap, so C=C bonds do not rotate freely. That is why cis/trans isomers exist.

s character: sp = 50%, sp² = 33%, sp³ = 25%. More s character means shorter, stronger bonds (C≡C shorter than C=C shorter than C–C) and more acidic C–H bonds (a terminal alkyne C–H is far more acidic than an alkane C–H).
Resonance changes hybridization: an atom with a lone pair next to a π bond is often sp² so the lone pair can delocalize. The amide N is planar, and the C–N bond has partial double-bond character.
Molecular polarity depends on shape: polar bonds can cancel in symmetric shapes (CO₂ is linear, so it is nonpolar), but not in bent or pyramidal ones (H₂O, NH₃).

ex.q: Acrylonitrile is CH₂=CH–C≡N. How many σ and π bonds does it have, and what is the hybridization of the nitrile carbon? (A) 6 σ, 3 π; sp (B) 5 σ, 3 π; sp² (C) 6 σ, 2 π; sp (D) 9 σ, 0 π; sp³
steps: Count σ bonds: 3 C–H, plus 1 σ in C=C, 1 σ in C–C, and 1 σ in C≡N = 6 σ.
Count π bonds: 1 in C=C and 2 in C≡N = 3 π.
The nitrile carbon has two σ bonds (to C and to N) and no lone pairs, so steric number 2 → sp. Answer: (A).

trap: Students count each double or triple bond as all σ or forget that every bond, multiple or not, contains exactly one σ. Count one σ per pair of bonded atoms first, then add the extra π bonds.
memory: Count the groups, not the bonds: 4 groups sp³, 3 groups sp², 2 groups sp.

why: Reaction mechanisms run through every Chem/Phys organic passage, where you must predict products, rates or stereochemistry from the substrate, nucleophile and solvent.
big: Nucleophiles and electrophiles: a nucleophile is electron-rich and donates a pair; an electrophile is electron-poor and accepts it. Curved arrows always start at electrons (a lone pair or bond) and point to where they go.
Leaving groups: the best leaving groups are weak, stable bases (I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ >> F⁻; tosylate and water are good). OH⁻ is poor unless it is protonated to H₂O.

SN2: one concerted step with backside attack, so the stereocenter inverts. Rate = k[Nu][RX]; methyl > 1° > 2° (3° does not react); favored by strong nucleophiles in polar aprotic solvents (DMSO, acetone).

SN1: the leaving group leaves first to form a carbocation, then the nucleophile attacks either face (racemization). Rate = k[RX]; 3° > 2°; favored by weak nucleophiles in polar protic solvents. Carbocations can rearrange (hydride or methyl shift) to a more stable cation.

Elimination: E2 is one step with a strong base and needs anti-periplanar H and leaving group; E1 goes through a carbocation. Heat favors elimination. Small strong bases usually give the more substituted alkene (Zaitsev), but bulky bases such as tert-butoxide give mostly the less substituted alkene (Hofmann).
Energetics: ΔH ≈ bonds broken − bonds formed (using bond dissociation energies). The slowest step, with the highest transition state, sets the rate.

ex.q: (R)-2-Bromobutane is treated with NaCN in DMSO. What is the main product? (A) Racemic 2-methylbutanenitrile (B) (S)-2-methylbutanenitrile (C) (R)-2-methylbutanenitrile (D) Mostly but-2-ene
steps: The substrate is secondary, CN⁻ is a strong nucleophile and weak base, and DMSO is polar aprotic, so SN2 wins.
SN2 backside attack inverts the stereocenter, which rules out racemic (A) and retention (C).
CN takes over bromine's top priority rank, so inverting the geometry flips the label from R to S. Answer: (B).

trap: Students often call any secondary substrate SN1. Decide from the full set of conditions: a strong nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent points to SN2, while a weak nucleophile in a protic solvent such as water or ethanol points to SN1.
memory: SN2 = 2 partners in one step, upside-down (inversion); SN1 = 1 partner in the slow step, a flat cation, both faces.

why: Alcohols appear in Chem/Phys and Bio/Biochem passages on synthesis, metabolism (ethanol to acetaldehyde) and lab identification, so you need to predict their properties and oxidation products.
big: Hydrogen bonding: the –OH group gives alcohols much higher boiling points than alkanes or ethers of similar mass, and small alcohols mix with water. More –OH groups mean higher boiling point.
Classifying alcohols: primary (1°), secondary (2°) or tertiary (3°) depends on how many carbons are attached to the carbon bearing the –OH.
Oxidation: 1° → aldehyde with mild PCC, or → carboxylic acid with strong oxidants (chromic acid/Jones, KMnO₄); 2° → ketone; 3° does not oxidize (no H on the carbinol carbon).

Acidity: simple alcohols have pKa ≈ 16, about like water. Phenols (pKa ≈ 10) are far more acidic because the phenoxide's charge is spread by resonance; electron-withdrawing groups raise acidity further.
–OH is a poor leaving group: make it a good one by protonating it in acid (leaves as H₂O), converting it to a tosylate or mesylate, or swapping it for a halide with SOCl₂ or PBr₃.
Protecting groups: an –OH can be masked as a silyl ether (e.g., TBDMS) so it survives other reactions, then removed later.

ex.q: Which alcohol gives a ketone when treated with PCC? (A) Butan-1-ol (B) Butan-2-ol (C) 2-Methylpropan-2-ol (D) Methanol
steps: Classify each: butan-1-ol and methanol are primary; butan-2-ol is secondary; 2-methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary.
PCC turns primary alcohols into aldehydes (methanol gives formaldehyde), turns secondary alcohols into ketones, and leaves tertiary alcohols alone.
Only butan-2-ol gives a ketone (butan-2-one). Answer (B).

trap: Students expect PCC to take a primary alcohol all the way to a carboxylic acid. PCC is the mild oxidant that stops at the aldehyde; chromic acid and KMnO₄ go on to the acid.
memory: Count the H's on the –OH carbon: 2 H's (1°) can oxidize twice, 1 H (2°) once, 0 H (3°) never.

why: Carbonyl reactions are the core of organic chemistry on the MCAT and appear in Chem/Phys and Bio/Biochem passages on sugars (hemiacetals), imines, and metabolism.
big: The carbonyl carbon is electrophilic: oxygen pulls electron density, leaving carbon δ+. Nucleophiles add to it, forming a tetrahedral intermediate (sp² becomes sp³).
Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones: they have less steric crowding and only one electron-donating alkyl group, so their carbonyl carbon is more δ+.

Alcohol addition: one alcohol gives a hemiacetal; a second (with acid catalyst, removing water) gives an acetal. Acetals are stable in base, so they serve as protecting groups; aqueous acid reverses them.
Nitrogen addition: a primary amine (RNH₂) gives an imine (C=N); a secondary amine gives an enamine. Both lose water.
Redox: NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄ reduces aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols. Aldehydes oxidize to carboxylic acids (positive Tollens test); ketones resist oxidation.
Carbon nucleophiles: Grignard reagents (RMgX) and cyanide (HCN gives a cyanohydrin) form new C–C bonds at the carbonyl carbon.

ex.q: Cyclohexanone is heated with excess methanol and a trace of H₂SO₄ while water is removed. What is the main product? (A) Cyclohexanol (B) A hemiacetal (C) 1,1-Dimethoxycyclohexane, an acetal (D) Methyl cyclohexanecarboxylate
steps: Acid protonates the carbonyl oxygen, making the carbon a better electrophile; methanol adds to give a hemiacetal.
With excess methanol and water being removed, the OH is protonated, leaves as water, and a second methanol adds.
The product has two OCH₃ groups on the former carbonyl carbon: an acetal. No reducing agent was present, so (A) is out. Answer: (C).

trap: Students stop at the hemiacetal. Excess alcohol plus acid and water removal drive the reaction to the acetal; a hemiacetal is the usual stopping point only when it is intramolecular, as in cyclic sugars.
memory: Carbonyl = target: nucleophiles hit the δ+ carbon, and the less crowded the target (aldehyde), the faster the hit.

why: Enols and enolates are how carbonyl compounds form new C–C bonds, so Chem/Phys and Bio/Biochem passages use them in aldol reactions, keto–enol tautomerism and metabolic steps such as the aldolase reaction in glycolysis.
big: α-carbon: the carbon next to a C=O. Its hydrogens are acidic (pKa ≈ 20 for ketones) because the enolate that forms is resonance-stabilized, with the negative charge shared onto oxygen.

Keto–enol tautomerism: an α-H moves to the oxygen and the C=O becomes C=C–OH. Acid or base catalyzes it, and the keto form usually dominates. Tautomers are different compounds, not resonance structures.
β-dicarbonyls (an α-H flanked by two C=O groups) are far more acidic (pKa ≈ 9–11) because the charge spreads over both oxygens.

Kinetic vs thermodynamic enolate: a bulky strong base at low temperature (LDA, −78 °C) removes the more accessible H on the less substituted α-carbon (kinetic). Weaker bases with heat and equilibrium give the more substituted, more stable enolate (thermodynamic).
Aldol reaction: an enolate (nucleophile) attacks another carbonyl carbon (electrophile) to give a β-hydroxy carbonyl. Heating dehydrates it to an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl (aldol condensation).
Racemization: a chiral α-carbon loses its configuration through the planar enol or enolate. A compound with no α-H cannot form an enolate.

ex.q: 2-Methylcyclohexanone is treated with LDA at −78 °C and then with CH₃I. Where is the new methyl group added? (A) C2, giving 2,2-dimethylcyclohexanone (B) C6, giving 2,6-dimethylcyclohexanone (C) on oxygen (D) C3
steps: The α-carbons are C2 (it already carries a CH₃ and has one H) and C6 (CH₂, two H).
LDA is bulky and strong, and the cold temperature makes deprotonation fast and irreversible, so it removes an H from the less hindered C6 (the kinetic enolate).
The enolate carbon attacks CH₃I in an SN2 reaction.
Answer: (B) 2,6-dimethylcyclohexanone.

trap: Students treat the enol and keto forms as resonance structures. They are tautomers, so atoms (an H) actually move. Also check for α-hydrogens before you predict any enolate chemistry.
memory: LDA, cold, and bulky: less substituted side (kinetic). Heat and time: more substituted side (thermodynamic).

why: Carboxylic acids appear in Chemical and Physical Foundations and Bio/Biochem passages on acidity, extractions, amino acids, fatty acids and ester or amide synthesis.
big: Acidity: most carboxylic acids have pKa about 4–5 because the carboxylate anion is stabilized by resonance over two oxygens. They are far more acidic than alcohols (pKa about 16).
Electron-withdrawing groups (Cl, F, NO₂) near the carboxyl group lower the pKa by induction; the effect grows with electronegativity and number of groups and fades with distance.
Hydrogen-bonded dimers give carboxylic acids higher boiling points than alcohols of similar mass.
Fischer esterification: acid + alcohol with an acid catalyst gives an ester + water. It is an equilibrium; push it forward with excess alcohol or by removing water.
Nucleophilic acyl substitution: SOCl₂ turns the acid into an acyl chloride, which then makes esters, amides and anhydrides easily.
Reduction: LiAlH₄ reduces a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol; NaBH₄ is too weak. β-keto acids lose CO₂ on heating (decarboxylation).

ex.q: A student heats butanoic acid with methanol and a little H₂SO₄ to make methyl butanoate. Which change would most increase the yield of ester? (A) Adding water (B) Using methanol as the solvent (C) Replacing H₂SO₄ with NaOH (D) Adding NaBH₄
steps: Fischer esterification is an equilibrium: acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water.
Adding water pushes it backward (Le Châtelier). NaOH turns the acid into carboxylate, which resists nucleophilic attack. NaBH₄ does not react usefully with the acid.
A large excess of methanol pushes the equilibrium toward the ester, so the answer is (B).

trap: Students treat Fischer esterification as going to completion and miss questions about driving it forward. Remember it is reversible, and that base stops it by forming the unreactive carboxylate ion.
memory: Carboxylate shares its charge between two oxygens, so sharing makes it stable and the acid strong (for an organic acid).

why: Acid derivatives show up in Chem/Phys and Bio/Biochem passages on ester and amide hydrolysis, soap making, peptide bonds, drug metabolism and acyl carriers like acetyl-CoA.
big: Reactivity order: acid chloride > anhydride > thioester > ester > amide. Reactions run easily downhill (more reactive → less reactive); going uphill needs an activating reagent.

Why the order: a better leaving group (a weaker base: Cl⁻ best) makes the carbonyl more reactive, while resonance donation into C=O makes it less reactive. Nitrogen donates its lone pair most strongly, so amides are the least reactive.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution: the nucleophile adds to the C=O to form a tetrahedral intermediate, then C=O re-forms and the leaving group leaves. Aldehydes and ketones have no leaving group, so they stop at addition.

Hydrolysis: esters + NaOH (saponification) → carboxylate salt + alcohol, which is irreversible because the carboxylate is deprotonated. Amides need strong acid or base and heat. Transesterification swaps an ester's alkoxy group for another alcohol's.
Reduction: LiAlH₄ reduces esters to primary alcohols and amides to amines.
Biology link: cells carry acyl groups as thioesters (acetyl-CoA) because they are reactive enough to transfer, while the amide peptide bond is stable enough to hold proteins together.

ex.q: Acetic anhydride, (CH₃CO)₂O, is mixed with methylamine, CH₃NH₂. What forms? (A) N-methylacetamide and acetic acid (B) methyl acetate and acetamide (C) two molecules of acetamide (D) No reaction, because amides are uphill from anhydrides
steps: An anhydride is more reactive than an amide, so anhydride → amide is downhill and goes on mixing. This rules out (D).
The amine nitrogen attacks one carbonyl, forming a tetrahedral intermediate. The C=O re-forms and acetate leaves.
The products are CH₃CONHCH₃ (N-methylacetamide) and acetic acid, which excess amine turns into a methylammonium acetate salt. Answer: (A).

trap: Students treat acyl carbons like alkyl halides and draw backside SN2 attack. The C=O is planar, so the nucleophile adds first and the leaving group leaves second.
memory: Downhill is easy: Chlorides → Anhydrides → Esters → Amides ("Can Anyone Ever Argue?").

why: Amines, amides, amino acids and phosphate bonds are the chemistry of proteins, DNA and ATP, so they appear in Chem/Phys and Bio/Biochem passages on biomolecules and synthesis.
big: Amines are bases because nitrogen has a lone pair. Alkyl amines (conjugate acid pKa about 10–11) are much more basic than aniline (about 4.6), whose lone pair is spread into the ring.
Amides are not basic: the nitrogen lone pair is shared by resonance with the C=O. This also makes the peptide bond planar and rigid.
Amino acids are zwitterions near neutral pH. For a neutral side chain, pI = (pKa₁ + pKa₂)/2; below the pI the molecule is net positive, above it net negative.
Making amines: Gabriel synthesis (phthalimide + alkyl halide gives a clean primary amine) and reductive amination (aldehyde or ketone + amine, then reduce the imine).
Phosphate bonds: a phosphoester links phosphate to an alcohol (DNA backbone); a phosphoanhydride links two phosphates (ATP has two). Hydrolyzing anhydride bonds releases much free energy.
Amines as salts: adding acid turns an amine into a water-soluble ammonium salt, the basis of acid–base extraction.

ex.q: Rank from most to least basic: ethylamine (CH₃CH₂NH₂), aniline (C₆H₅NH₂), acetamide (CH₃CONH₂). (A) aniline > ethylamine > acetamide (B) ethylamine > aniline > acetamide (C) acetamide > ethylamine > aniline (D) ethylamine > acetamide > aniline
steps: Ethylamine's lone pair sits on nitrogen and the ethyl group donates electrons, so it is the strongest base.
Aniline's lone pair is partly spread into the benzene ring, so it is weaker.
Acetamide's lone pair is tied up in resonance with C=O, so it is barely basic at all. Answer: (B).

trap: Students see an NH₂ group and call it basic. Always check what the nitrogen is attached to: next to a C=O (amide) or a ring (aniline), the lone pair is less available.
memory: A free lone pair makes a base; a shared lone pair makes a weak one.

why: Spectroscopy appears in Chem/Phys passages that ask you to identify a product or confirm a reaction worked, usually from an IR band, an NMR pattern or a mass spectrum peak.
big: IR spectroscopy detects bond vibrations. Memorize: C=O ≈ 1700 cm⁻¹ (strong, sharp); alcohol O–H 3200–3600 (broad); carboxylic acid O–H 2500–3300 (very broad, plus C=O); N–H ≈ 3300 (a primary amine shows two peaks); C≡N or C≡C ≈ 2100–2260.
¹H NMR signals: the number of signals = the number of unique H environments; integration = the relative number of H; splitting follows the n + 1 rule (n = H on neighboring carbons).

Chemical shift: electronegative neighbors deshield H and move it downfield (higher ppm). Rough values: alkyl 0.9–2; next to C=O 2–2.5; next to O 3.3–4; aromatic 6.5–8; aldehyde 9–10; carboxylic acid 10–12.
¹³C NMR gives one peak per unique carbon; carbonyl carbons appear far downfield (about 160–220 ppm).
Mass spectrometry sorts ions by m/z. The molecular ion gives the mass; Cl gives M and M+2 peaks in about 3:1 ratio, Br about 1:1. An ion with charge 2+ appears at about half its mass.
UV-Vis detects electronic transitions in conjugated π systems; more conjugation means a smaller energy gap and a longer wavelength of maximum absorption.

ex.q: A compound C₃H₆O shows a strong IR band at 1715 cm⁻¹ and no band near 3300 cm⁻¹. Its ¹H NMR shows a single singlet (6 H). What is it? (A) Propanal (B) Acetone (C) Prop-2-en-1-ol (D) Methyl vinyl ether
steps: 1715 cm⁻¹ means C=O, which rules out the alcohol (C) and the ether (D); the missing 3300 band also rules out an O–H.
Propanal (CH₃CH₂CHO) would show three NMR signals, including an aldehyde H near 9–10 ppm.
One 6 H singlet means two identical CH₃ groups with no H neighbors: (CH₃)₂C=O. Answer: (B).

trap: Students mistake any peak near 3000 cm⁻¹ for O–H. C–H stretches sit right around 3000 and are in nearly every organic spectrum; an O–H is broad and higher (about 3200–3600), or very broad and lower for a carboxylic acid.
memory: IR finds the functional group; NMR finds the neighbors.

why: Lab-technique passages in Chem/Phys ask how a chemist isolated or purified a product, so you must link polarity, acidity and boiling point to each method.
big: Extraction separates by solubility: charged species go into the aqueous layer, neutral organics stay in the organic layer. Like dissolves like.
Acid–base extraction: aqueous HCl pulls out amines (as ammonium salts); NaHCO₃ (weak base) pulls out carboxylic acids (pKa ≈ 4–5); NaOH (strong base) also pulls out phenols (pKa ≈ 10).

Distillation separates by boiling point. Simple distillation works when boiling points differ by more than about 25 °C; fractional distillation handles closer boiling points; vacuum distillation lowers boiling points for heat-sensitive or very high-boiling compounds.

Chromatography: on normal-phase silica (polar stationary phase), polar compounds stick and move less. Rf = distance traveled by spot ÷ distance traveled by solvent front, so the least polar compound has the highest Rf. Reverse-phase is the opposite.

Other column methods: size-exclusion elutes the largest molecules first; ion-exchange separates by charge; affinity chromatography uses a specific binding partner; gas chromatography separates volatile compounds by boiling point and polarity.
Recrystallization purifies a solid: dissolve it in a minimum of hot solvent in which it is soluble hot but poorly soluble cold, then cool slowly so impurities stay in solution.

ex.q: An ether solution contains aniline, benzoic acid, phenol and naphthalene. It is washed in turn with aqueous HCl, then NaHCO₃, then NaOH. Which compound is in the NaOH layer? (A) Aniline (B) Benzoic acid (C) Phenol (D) Naphthalene
steps: HCl protonates the basic amine, so aniline leaves first as anilinium chloride.
NaHCO₃ is basic enough to deprotonate benzoic acid (pKa ≈ 4.2) but not phenol (pKa ≈ 10), so benzoate leaves next.
NaOH deprotonates phenol to water-soluble phenoxide; neutral naphthalene stays in the ether. Answer: (C).

trap: Students forget that the stationary phase decides the order on TLC. On polar silica the polar compound has the lower Rf; check which phase is polar before you rank spots.
memory: Charged goes to water; polar sticks to silica; big runs first in size-exclusion.

why: Motion and forces underlie much of the physics in Chem/Phys, often set in medical contexts such as falling objects, joints acting as levers, or patients on inclined beds.
big: Kinematics (constant acceleration): v = v₀ + at; Δx = v₀t + ½at²; v² = v₀² + 2aΔx. Use g ≈ 10 m/s² for estimates.
Vectors: split forces and velocities into components (F_x = F cos θ, F_y = F sin θ). Know sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° ≈ 0.87, sin 45° = cos 45° ≈ 0.71.
Newton's laws: an object keeps its velocity unless a net force acts (inertia); F_net = ma; every force has an equal and opposite partner acting on the other object.

Common forces: weight = mg; normal force acts perpendicular to the surface (mg cos θ on a simple incline); friction f_s ≤ μ_sN and f_k = μ_kN; on an incline the downhill component of gravity is mg sin θ.
Projectiles: horizontal velocity stays constant (no air resistance); vertical motion has a = −g. Time in the air is set by the vertical motion alone.
Torque and equilibrium: τ = rF sin θ. In equilibrium, net force = 0 and net torque = 0, so clockwise torques equal counterclockwise torques.

ex.q: A box starts from rest at the top of a frictionless ramp inclined at 30°. What is its speed after 2.0 s? (Use g = 10 m/s².) (A) 5.0 m/s (B) 8.7 m/s (C) 10 m/s (D) 20 m/s
steps: Only the component of gravity along the ramp accelerates the box: a = g sin 30° = 10 × 0.5 = 5.0 m/s².
From rest, v = at = 5.0 × 2.0 = 10 m/s. Answer (C).

trap: Assuming the normal force always equals mg. On an incline it is mg cos θ, and an extra push or pull at an angle changes it again; draw a free-body diagram first.
memory: Sin slides you down: the force along a ramp is mg sin θ; the normal force is mg cos θ.

why: Work and energy are tested in Chem/Phys passages on lifting, falling, springs, friction, and power use in medical devices.
big: Work: W = Fd cos θ, measured in joules (1 J = 1 N·m). A force perpendicular to the motion (like a centripetal force) does zero work.
Kinetic and potential energy: KE = ½mv², gravitational PE = mgh, spring PE = ½kx².
Work-energy theorem: net work on an object equals its change in kinetic energy, W(net) = ΔKE.
Conservation of mechanical energy: with only conservative forces (gravity, springs), KE + PE stays constant. Friction and air resistance are nonconservative and turn mechanical energy into heat.
Power: P = W/t = Fv, in watts (1 W = 1 J/s). Energy = power × time, so 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

ex.q: A 2.0 kg sled starts from rest at the top of a hill 5.0 m high and reaches the bottom at 8.0 m/s. How much mechanical energy was lost to friction? (Use g = 10 m/s².) (A) 16 J (B) 36 J (C) 64 J (D) 100 J
steps: Starting energy: PE = mgh = (2.0)(10)(5.0) = 100 J; KE = 0.
Final energy: KE = ½(2.0)(8.0)² = 64 J; PE = 0.
Energy lost = 100 J − 64 J = 36 J. Answer: (B).

trap: Students multiply force by any distance. Only the component of displacement along the force counts; for gravity, use the vertical height, not the length of the ramp.
memory: Energy is money: it can change form (PE to KE to heat), but you can always account for every joule.

why: Thermodynamics links heat, work and energy, so Chem/Phys passages on engines, gas expansions, calorimetry and body heat balance ask you to apply the first law and track signs.
big: Zeroth law: if A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are at the same temperature, and no net heat flows between them.
First law: ΔU = Q − W, where Q is heat added to the system and W is work done by the system. Chemistry often writes ΔU = q + w, with w as work done on the system. Both say the same thing.
Gas work: at constant pressure, W = PΔV. On a P–V graph, work is the area under the curve. No volume change means no work.
Special processes: isothermal (ideal gas): ΔU = 0, so Q = W. Adiabatic: Q = 0, so ΔU = −W. Isochoric: W = 0, so ΔU = Q. Isobaric: P is constant.
Heat and phase change: q = mcΔT within a phase, and q = mL during a phase change, when the temperature stays constant. Heat moves by conduction, convection and radiation.
Second law: the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases, and heat flows on its own from hot to cold. No engine is 100% efficient.

ex.q: A gas in a cylinder absorbs 400 J of heat and expands at a constant pressure of 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa from 1.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³. What is ΔU of the gas? (A) +600 J (B) +400 J (C) +200 J (D) −200 J
steps: Work done by the gas: W = PΔV = (2.0 × 10⁵ Pa)(1.0 × 10⁻³ m³) = 2.0 × 10² J = 200 J.
First law: ΔU = Q − W = 400 J − 200 J.
Answer: (C) +200 J. Half the heat went into internal energy and half into pushing the piston.

trap: Sign errors cause most wrong answers. Decide first whether W means work done by the gas or on it, then use the matching form of the first law. Expansion means the gas does work, and that drains internal energy.
memory: Heat in is +Q. Work out (expansion) takes energy away from U.

why: Fluids show up in Chemical and Physical Foundations passages on blood flow, blood pressure, diving, IV bags and lab density measurements.
big: Density ρ = m/V; water is 1000 kg/m³ = 1 g/cm³. Specific gravity = ρ ÷ ρwater, with no units.
Hydrostatic pressure: P = P₀ + ρgh. Gauge pressure = ρgh, the pressure above atmospheric. About every 10 m of water adds 1 atm (≈ 1 × 10⁵ Pa).
Buoyant force (Archimedes): Fb = ρfluid × Vsubmerged × g, equal to the weight of displaced fluid. A floating object has fraction submerged = ρobject ÷ ρfluid.
Pascal's principle: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted everywhere; a hydraulic lift gives F₂ = F₁ × (A₂/A₁).
Continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, so fluid speeds up where a tube narrows. Bernoulli: P + ½ρv² + ρgh is constant, so faster flow means lower pressure.
Poiseuille's law: Q = πr⁴ΔP/(8ηL). Flow depends on radius to the fourth power, so halving r cuts flow to 1/16.

ex.q: A 0.0020 m³ metal block (density 3000 kg/m³) hangs from a spring scale, fully submerged in water (1000 kg/m³). What does the scale read? (g = 10 m/s²) (A) 20 N (B) 40 N (C) 60 N (D) 80 N
steps: Buoyant force = 1000 × 0.0020 × 10 = 20 N, pushing up.
Scale reading = 60 − 20 = 40 N, so the answer is (B).

trap: Students plug the object's density into the buoyant-force equation. Fb always uses the fluid's density and the submerged volume; the object's density only decides whether it sinks or floats.
memory: Buoyancy belongs to the fluid: weigh the water you push aside.

why: Electrostatics and magnetism appear in Chem/Phys passages on charged particles, nerve membranes, mass spectrometers and medical devices, usually as ratio or proportion reasoning without a calculator.
big: Coulomb's law: F = kq₁q₂/r², with k ≈ 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². Like charges repel and opposite charges attract. Doubling r cuts F to 1/4; tripling r cuts it to 1/9.
Electric field: E = F/q = kQ/r² (N/C, same as V/m). It points away from + charges and toward − charges. A positive charge is pushed along E; a negative charge is pushed the opposite way.

Potential and energy: V = kQ/r is a scalar; U = qV. Work done by the field = −qΔV. Positive charges move on their own toward lower V; negative charges move toward higher V. In a uniform field, ΔV = Ed. Equipotential lines are perpendicular to field lines.
Charge is conserved and quantized: q = ne, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Identical conducting spheres that touch end up sharing the total charge equally.

Magnetic force: F = qvB sin θ, perpendicular to both v and B (right-hand rule). It is zero for motion parallel to B. Because it is perpendicular to v, it does no work: it bends the path (r = mv/qB) without changing speed.
Currents make magnetic fields: around a straight wire the field lines are circles, B = μ₀I/(2πr).

ex.q: A proton (q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) starts at rest and is accelerated through a potential difference of 500 V. How much kinetic energy does it gain? (A) 3.2 × 10⁻²² J (B) 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (C) 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁷ J (D) 500 J
steps: Energy conservation: the electric potential energy lost equals the kinetic energy gained, so KE = qΔV.
Estimate: 1.6 × 5 = 8, and 10⁻¹⁹ × 10² = 10⁻¹⁷. So KE = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁷ J (which is 500 eV).
Answer: (C). Choice (A) comes from dividing instead of multiplying.

trap: Students forget the sign of the charge: electrons move opposite to E and toward higher potential. Decide the direction from the sign first, then do the magnitude.
memory: Fields are arrows, potentials are just numbers: add fields as vectors, add potentials like money.

why: Circuits show up in Chem/Phys passages on lab equipment, nerve membranes modeled as resistors and capacitors, and devices like defibrillators.
big: Ohm's law: V = IR. Current is flow of charge (I = Q/t); resistance of a wire is R = ρL/A, so longer, thinner wires resist more.
Series resistors add (R = R₁ + R₂) and carry the same current. Parallel resistors combine as 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂, share the same voltage, and the total is smaller than the smallest one.
Kirchhoff's rules: current into a junction equals current out; voltage gains and drops around any closed loop add to zero.
Power: P = IV = I²R = V²/R, measured in watts (J/s).
Capacitors: Q = CV, C = κε₀A/d, stored energy U = ½CV². Capacitors combine opposite to resistors: add in parallel, reciprocals in series.
Meters: an ammeter goes in series (ideally zero resistance); a voltmeter goes in parallel (ideally infinite resistance).

ex.q: A 12 V battery is connected to a 2 Ω resistor in series with two 4 Ω resistors that are in parallel with each other. What is the current through one of the 4 Ω resistors? (A) 0.75 A (B) 1.5 A (C) 3.0 A (D) 6.0 A
steps: Two equal 4 Ω resistors in parallel give 4/2 = 2 Ω.
Total resistance = 2 Ω + 2 Ω = 4 Ω, so total current I = 12 V / 4 Ω = 3 A.
All 3 A flows into the parallel pair and splits evenly between the two equal branches.
Each 4 Ω resistor carries 1.5 A. Answer: (B).

trap: Students mix up the rules and add parallel resistances directly, or use the series rule for capacitors. Remember that adding a parallel path always lowers total resistance.
memory: Series shares current, parallel shares voltage; capacitors do the opposite of resistors.

why: Waves and sound show up in Chem/Phys passages on ultrasound, hearing, Doppler blood-flow measurement and musical instruments, often with a quick v = fλ or decibel calculation.
big: Wave speed: v = fλ and f = 1/T. The medium sets the speed; the source sets the frequency, and frequency stays the same when a wave enters a new medium (wavelength changes instead).

Transverse vs. longitudinal: sound is a longitudinal pressure wave, so it cannot be polarized. Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases (about 343 m s⁻¹ in room-temperature air, about 1500 m s⁻¹ in water).
Sound level: β = 10 log(I/I₀) in decibels. Each factor of 10 in intensity adds 10 dB. From a point source, I ∝ 1/r², so doubling distance cuts intensity to 1/4.
Doppler effect: f′ = f (v ± v_observer)/(v ∓ v_source). When source and observer move toward each other the heard frequency is higher; when they move apart it is lower.
Standing waves: strings fixed at both ends and pipes open at both ends have λ = 2L/n (n = 1, 2, 3 …). A pipe closed at one end has λ = 4L/n with odd n only.
Interference and beats: crest meets crest is constructive; crest meets trough is destructive. Two close frequencies produce beats at f_beat = |f₁ − f₂|.

ex.q: An organ pipe open at both ends is 0.85 m long. If the speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹, what is its fundamental frequency? (A) 50 Hz (B) 100 Hz (C) 200 Hz (D) 400 Hz
steps: Open at both ends, fundamental (n = 1): λ = 2L = 2 × 0.85 m = 1.7 m.
Check: if the pipe were closed at one end, λ = 4L = 3.4 m and f = 100 Hz, which is choice (B), the common wrong answer.

trap: Students think raising the frequency makes sound travel faster. In a given medium speed is fixed, so a higher frequency just means a shorter wavelength.
memory: Closed pipe: quarter wave (4L); open pipe or string: half wave (2L).

why: Optics appears in Chem/Phys passages on the eye, microscopes, fiber-optic endoscopes and spectroscopy, often as a lens-equation calculation or a ray-behavior question.
big: Light as a wave and photon: c = fλ and E = hf = hc/λ, with hc ≈ 1240 eV·nm. Shorter wavelength means higher energy (radio < IR < visible < UV < X-ray < gamma).
Refraction: n = c/v and Snell's law n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂. Entering a denser medium, light slows and bends toward the normal; frequency never changes, so wavelength shortens.
Total internal reflection happens only when light goes from higher n to lower n at an angle above the critical angle, where sinθc = n₂/n₁.
Thin lens and mirror equation: 1/f = 1/do + 1/di and m = −di/do. For mirrors f = R/2. Lens power P = 1/f in diopters (f in meters).
Sign conventions: converging lenses and concave mirrors have f > 0; diverging lenses and convex mirrors have f < 0. Positive di means a real, inverted image; negative di means virtual and upright.
Diverging lenses and convex mirrors always give virtual, upright, reduced images. Nearsightedness is corrected with diverging lenses, farsightedness with converging lenses.

ex.q: An object is 5.0 cm from a converging lens with f = 10 cm. Describe the image. (A) Real, inverted, 2× size (B) Virtual, upright, 2× size (C) Real, upright, half size (D) No image forms
steps: Negative di means the image is virtual, on the same side as the object.
m = −di/do = −(−10)/5 = +2: upright and twice as large, like a magnifying glass. Answer: (B).

trap: Students lose signs: they forget that a diverging lens has a negative f or read a negative di as an error. Write the sign on f first and let the sign of di tell you real or virtual.
memory: For one lens or mirror: real is inverted, virtual is upright. Inside the focal point of a converging lens, you get a magnifying glass.

why: Atomic and nuclear physics appears in Chem/Phys passages on medical imaging, radioactive tracers, radiation therapy and emission spectra.
big: Nuclear notation: ᴬ_Z X, where Z is protons and A is protons + neutrons. In every nuclear equation, A and Z each add up to the same total on both sides.

Decay types: alpha (⁴₂He) lowers A by 4 and Z by 2; β⁻ turns a neutron into a proton (Z + 1, A same); β⁺ and electron capture turn a proton into a neutron (Z − 1, A same); gamma releases energy with no change in A or Z.
Half-life: N = N₀(½)^(t/T½). After 1, 2, 3 half-lives, ½, ¼, ⅛ remains. Decay is first order, so the half-life does not depend on how much you start with.

Mass defect and binding energy: a nucleus weighs less than its separate nucleons; the missing mass is binding energy, E = mc² (1 u ≈ 931 MeV). Fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei both release energy.
Photoelectric effect: KE_max = hf − φ. Below the threshold frequency no electrons are ejected, however bright the light; brightness changes how many electrons, not their energy.
Penetration and deflection: alpha is stopped by paper, beta by thin metal, gamma needs thick lead. In a field, alpha and β⁻ bend opposite ways and gamma goes straight.

ex.q: Uranium-238 (Z = 92) undergoes one alpha decay followed by two β⁻ decays. What is the final nucleus? (A) Thorium-234 (Z = 90) (B) Protactinium-234 (Z = 91) (C) Uranium-234 (Z = 92) (D) Uranium-238 (Z = 92)
steps: Alpha decay: A = 238 − 4 = 234, Z = 92 − 2 = 90 (thorium-234).
Each β⁻ raises Z by 1 and leaves A unchanged: Z goes 90 → 91 → 92, A stays 234.
Z = 92 is uranium again, so the product is uranium-234, an isotope of the parent. Answer (C).

trap: Mixing up β⁻ and β⁺: β⁻ emits an electron and raises Z; β⁺ emits a positron and lowers Z. Write the balanced equation and check that A and Z match on both sides.
memory: Alpha: minus 4, minus 2. Beta-minus: Z goes up (a neutron becomes a proton).

why: There is no calculator on the MCAT, so fast estimation, scientific notation, and logs decide your speed on every science section.
big: Scientific notation: multiply the coefficients and add the exponents; divide the coefficients and subtract the exponents. (2 × 10³)(4 × 10⁻⁵) = 8 × 10⁻².
Rounding to estimate: round to easy numbers, then pick the closest choice. Answer choices are usually spread far enough apart for this to work.
Logarithms: log(10ⁿ) = n, log(ab) = log a + log b, log 2 ≈ 0.3, log 3 ≈ 0.48. So −log(2 × 10⁻⁴) = 4 − 0.3 = 3.7.
Units and conversions: carry units through every step and cancel them like numbers. Know metric prefixes: milli 10⁻³, micro 10⁻⁶, nano 10⁻⁹, kilo 10³.
Proportional reasoning: if y ∝ x², doubling x makes y four times larger; if y ∝ 1/r², doubling r makes y one quarter as large.
Significant figures: report a product or quotient with as many sig figs as the least precise measurement.

steps: Round the coefficients: 3.1 ≈ 3 and 5.9 ≈ 6, so the top is about 18 × 10² = 1.8 × 10³.
The exact value is about 0.91, so the estimate is safe. Answer: (B).

trap: Students lose track of exponents when dividing, especially with negative powers. Write the powers of ten on a separate line and handle them last.
memory: Round first, compute second, check the order of magnitude third.

why: Every science section includes experiment-based passages, and the MCAT asks you to identify variables, spot confounds and judge what a study can and cannot conclude. This is the 'Scientific Inquiry and Reasoning' skill.
big: Independent variable (IV): what the researcher manipulates. Dependent variable (DV): what is measured. Controlled variables are held constant, and a control group shows what happens without the treatment.

Experimental vs observational: only a randomized experiment can support a cause-and-effect claim. Observational designs (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional) show associations: correlation is not causation.
Confound: a third variable linked to both the IV and the DV that offers another explanation. Random assignment spreads confounds evenly across groups and protects internal validity.
Random sampling (who enters the study) supports external validity (generalizing to the population). It is a different thing from random assignment (who gets which treatment).
Bias control: placebos and blinding (single- or double-blind) reduce expectation effects. Watch for selection bias, attrition and the Hawthorne effect.
Ethics (Belmont principles): respect for persons (informed consent), beneficence (maximize benefit, minimize harm) and justice (fair selection of participants).

ex.q: Students who chose to join an optional study group scored 12 points higher on the final than those who did not. A dean concludes the group raises scores. What is the strongest objection? (A) The sample was too small (B) Students chose for themselves, so motivation may explain the difference (C) No dependent variable was measured (D) The study was double-blind
steps: Group membership was not assigned. Students selected themselves, so the study is observational.
Motivated students are more likely both to join and to study hard, so motivation is a confound linked to both variables.
The fix would be randomly assigning students to the group or no group.
Answer: (B).

trap: Students mix up random sampling with random assignment. Sampling affects whom you can generalize to. Assignment is what lets you claim causation. Before you accept a causal conclusion, ask: was the IV manipulated and randomly assigned?
memory: No manipulation and no random assignment means no causation.

why: Every science section and Psych/Soc include passages with tables, graphs and statistical results, and many questions ask what the data do or do not show.
big: Mean, median, mode: the mean is pulled by outliers, the median is resistant to them, and the mode is the only center for categories (like insurance type).
Skew: in a right-skewed distribution (long tail to the right) the mean is greater than the median; in a left-skewed one it is less.
Standard deviation measures spread around the mean. In a normal distribution about 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values fall within 1, 2 and 3 SD of the mean.
p-value: the chance of results at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true. p < α (often 0.05) means statistically significant, which is not the same as large or important.
Type I error = rejecting a true null (false positive, rate α); Type II error = missing a real effect (false negative). Larger samples raise power and cut Type II errors.
Correlation (r from −1 to +1) shows strength and direction of a linear link, not causation. A 95% confidence interval that includes zero difference (or a ratio of 1) is not significant at p < 0.05.

ex.q: Systolic blood pressure in a large sample is normally distributed with mean 120 mmHg and SD 10 mmHg. About what percent of people have values above 140 mmHg? (A) 2.5% (B) 5% (C) 16% (D) 32%
steps: 140 is (140 − 120) ÷ 10 = 2 SD above the mean.
About 95% lie within ±2 SD, so 5% lie outside, split evenly between the two tails.
Upper tail = 5% ÷ 2 = 2.5%, so the answer is (A).

trap: Students read a significant p-value as proof of causation or of a big effect. Check the study design (randomized or observational) and the size of the difference before concluding anything.
memory: 68-95-99.7, and cut it in half for one tail.

why: Amino acids and proteins sit at the center of the Bio/Biochem section and also appear in Chem/Phys, often in passages on enzyme active sites, mutations, titration curves or protein folding.
big: Structure: the α-carbon holds an amino group, a carboxyl group, H and a side chain (R). Every amino acid except glycine is chiral. Natural ones are L, which is (S) for all of them except cysteine, which is (R).

Side-chain classes: nonpolar (G, A, V, L, I, M, F, W, P); polar uncharged (S, T, N, Q, C, Y); acidic and negative at pH 7.4 (D, E); basic and positive (K, R). Histidine (pKa ≈ 6) is mostly neutral at 7.4 and protonates in slightly acidic places.

Charge and pH: a group is protonated when the pH is below its pKa. Below the pI the net charge is positive; above the pI it is negative. At physiological pH a free amino acid is a zwitterion (−NH₃⁺, −COO⁻).
Peptide bond: an amide formed by condensation, which releases H₂O. It has partial double-bond character, so it is planar and rigid. Hydrolysis is favorable but very slow without a catalyst.

Levels of structure: primary = sequence; secondary = α-helix and β-sheet held by backbone N–H···O=C hydrogen bonds; tertiary = side-chain interactions (hydrophobic effect, disulfide bonds between cysteines, salt bridges); quaternary = subunits together. Proline breaks helices.
Denaturation by heat, pH extremes, urea or detergents breaks higher structure but leaves the peptide bonds (primary structure) intact.

ex.q: Aspartic acid has pKa values of 2.0 (α-COOH), 3.9 (side-chain COOH) and 9.9 (α-NH₃⁺). What is its isoelectric point? (A) 2.95 (B) 5.95 (C) 6.9 (D) 9.9
steps: Track the charge as pH rises from very low: +1 (fully protonated) → 0 after pKa 2.0 → −1 after pKa 3.9 → −2 after pKa 9.9.
The neutral (net 0) form exists between pKa 2.0 and pKa 3.9, so the pI is the average of those two.
pI = (2.0 + 3.9)/2 = 2.95. Answer: (A). Choice (B) averages the wrong pair of pKa values.

trap: Students average all the pKa values or the first and last ones. Instead, find the net-zero form and average only the two pKa values on either side of it.
memory: pH below pKa, the H stays on; pH above pKa, the H is gone.

why: Enzyme kinetics and inhibition are core Bio/Biochem content, often tested with passages built around a Michaelis–Menten or Lineweaver–Burk graph from an experiment or drug study.
big: Enzymes are catalysts: they lower activation energy and speed up both directions, but do not change ΔG, K or the final equilibrium.
Michaelis–Menten: v = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]). Km is the [S] that gives half of Vmax; a lower Km means higher apparent affinity.
Inhibitors: competitive raises Km, Vmax unchanged; noncompetitive lowers Vmax, Km unchanged; uncompetitive lowers both; mixed lowers Vmax and changes Km.
Lineweaver–Burk plots 1/v vs 1/[S]: y-intercept = 1/Vmax, x-intercept = −1/Km, slope = Km/Vmax.
kcat (turnover number) = Vmax/[E]total; kcat/Km measures catalytic efficiency.
Regulation: allosteric enzymes give sigmoidal curves (cooperativity); enzymes are also controlled by phosphorylation, zymogen cleavage and feedback inhibition.

ex.q: An enzyme has Vmax = 100 µmol/min and Km = 2 mM. What is the reaction rate when [S] = 6 mM? (A) 25 µmol/min (B) 50 µmol/min (C) 75 µmol/min (D) 100 µmol/min
steps: Plug into v = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]) = 100 × 6 / (2 + 6).
Check: [S] is 3 times Km, so v = 3/4 of Vmax. Answer: (C).

trap: Students say an enzyme makes a reaction more favorable. It only makes it faster; ΔG and K are untouched. Also, extra substrate can overcome a competitive inhibitor but not a noncompetitive one.
memory: Competitive competes for the site, so it messes with Km; noncompetitive knocks out enzyme, so it cuts Vmax.

why: Bio/Biochem passages often describe an experiment that separates or identifies proteins, and questions test which method was used, what a band or peak means, and how structure fits function.
big: Structural proteins: collagen (a triple helix rich in Gly and Pro; vitamin C is needed to make it), keratin, elastin, actin and tubulin. Their strength comes from repeating, ordered structure.
Motor proteins use ATP to move along tracks: myosin on actin; kinesin toward the plus end of microtubules (outward, toward the axon terminal); dynein toward the minus end (back toward the cell body).
Antibodies have two heavy and two light chains held by disulfide bonds. The variable regions at the tips bind antigen; the constant (Fc) region signals to immune cells.

Electrophoresis: SDS-PAGE denatures proteins and coats them with negative charge, so they separate by mass, with small proteins moving farthest. Native PAGE separates by size, shape and charge. A reducing agent (such as β-mercaptoethanol) breaks disulfide bonds.
Isoelectric point (pI): the pH where net charge is zero. When pH < pI the protein is positive; when pH > pI it is negative. Isoelectric focusing stops each protein at its pI.

Chromatography: size-exclusion elutes large proteins first; ion exchange binds proteins of opposite charge to the beads (cation exchange beads are negative and bind cations); affinity uses a specific ligand or antibody.

ex.q: A protein with pI = 5.0 is loaded onto a cation-exchange column at pH 7.0. What happens? (A) It binds tightly because it is positive (B) It flows through because it is negative (C) It binds because it is neutral (D) It is retained by size
steps: The buffer pH (7.0) is above the pI (5.0), so the protein has lost protons and carries a net negative charge.
A cation-exchange resin is negatively charged and holds positive proteins.
A negative protein is repelled and comes out in the flow-through. Answer: (B).

trap: Students mix up the column names: a cation exchanger binds cations, so its beads are negative. Name the charge of the protein first, then ask whether the beads are opposite.
memory: pH below pI, protein is positive ("low pH, plus charge").

why: Carbohydrate structure shows up in Bio/Biochem passages on digestion, metabolism, glycoproteins and lab sugar tests, often asking about stereochemistry, anomers or glycosidic bonds.
big: Monosaccharides are aldoses (aldehyde at C1, like glucose) or ketoses (ketone at C2, like fructose). D or L is set by the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl: OH on the right in a Fischer projection means D.
Stereoisomers: a sugar with n chiral centers has 2ⁿ stereoisomers. Epimers differ at only one carbon (glucose and galactose at C4; glucose and mannose at C2).

Cyclization forms a hemiacetal (or hemiketal), creating a new chiral anomeric carbon (C1 in glucose). For D-sugars in a Haworth drawing, α has the anomeric OH down and β has it up. Anomers interconvert in water (mutarotation).

Reducing sugars have a free anomeric carbon, so the ring can open to a free carbonyl and give a positive Benedict's or Tollens' test. All monosaccharides, including ketoses such as fructose (which tautomerizes to an aldose in base), are reducing. Sucrose is non-reducing because both anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond.
Glycosidic bonds join sugars: maltose is Glc α-1,4 Glc; lactose is Gal β-1,4 Glc; sucrose is Glc α-1,β-2 Fru.
Polysaccharides: starch (amylose, amylopectin) and glycogen use α-1,4 links with α-1,6 branches (glycogen branches more often); cellulose uses β-1,4 links, which human enzymes cannot digest.

ex.q: Ribose is a D-aldopentose. How many D-aldopentoses exist? (A) 2 (B) 4 (C) 8 (D) 16
steps: An open-chain aldopentose has chiral centers at C2, C3 and C4: 3 centers.
Total stereoisomers = 2³ = 8.
Half have the C4 OH on the right (D), so there are 4 D-aldopentoses (ribose, arabinose, xylose, lyxose). Answer: (B).

trap: Students mix up D/L with α/β. D/L is fixed by the carbon farthest from the carbonyl and never changes; α/β describes only the anomeric carbon and flips during mutarotation.
memory: Beta is up, like a bee flying up (for D-sugars in Haworth form).

why: Lipids appear in Bio/Biochem passages on membranes, energy storage, hormone signaling and fat digestion, and you need to link a lipid's structure to its function.
big: Fatty acids: long carboxylic acid chains. Saturated chains have no C=C and pack tightly (higher melting point); cis double bonds in unsaturated chains put kinks in the chain and lower the melting point. Notation 18:1 means 18 carbons, 1 double bond.
Triacylglycerols are glycerol esterified to three fatty acids. They are the main energy store, giving about 9 kcal/g versus about 4 kcal/g for carbohydrate or protein.

Phospholipids and sphingolipids are amphipathic (polar head, nonpolar tails). With two tails they form bilayers on their own in water, the basis of membranes; single-tailed lipids such as free fatty acids and bile salts form micelles instead.
Steroids have four fused rings. Cholesterol keeps membrane fluidity steady across temperatures and is the starting material for steroid hormones, bile acids and vitamin D.
Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K need fat and bile for absorption, and they can build up in the body. Terpenes are built from five-carbon isoprene units.
Eicosanoids such as prostaglandins are made from arachidonic acid and act as local signals for inflammation and pain; aspirin and NSAIDs block their synthesis by inhibiting COX.

ex.q: Which fatty acid has the highest melting point? (A) Linoleic acid, 18:2 (cis) (B) Oleic acid, 18:1 (cis) (C) Stearic acid, 18:0 (D) Palmitic acid, 16:0
steps: Saturated chains pack closely and have stronger London forces, so the saturated choices (C and D) melt higher than the unsaturated ones.
Between two saturated acids, the longer chain has more surface contact and stronger London forces: 18 carbons beat 16.
Stearic acid (18:0) melts highest. Answer (C).

trap: Thinking lipids are polymers made of repeating monomers like proteins or starch. Lipids are grouped by being hydrophobic, not by a shared building block, so judge each one by its structure.
memory: Straight chains stack like pencils (solid butter); kinked chains pile up loosely (liquid oil).

why: DNA structure, replication and lab methods like PCR and gel electrophoresis appear in Bio/Biochem passages built around experiments.
big: DNA structure: two antiparallel strands, each read 5′→3′, joined by base pairs. A–T has 2 hydrogen bonds and G–C has 3, so GC-rich DNA melts at higher temperature. Chargaff: A = T and G = C.
Replication is semiconservative. DNA polymerase needs a primer and adds nucleotides only to a free 3′-OH, so new DNA grows 5′→3′.
Leading and lagging strands: the leading strand is made continuously; the lagging strand is made in Okazaki fragments joined by DNA ligase. Helicase unwinds, primase lays RNA primers.
PCR repeats denature (about 95 °C), anneal primers (about 50–65 °C), and extend (about 72 °C, heat-stable polymerase). Each cycle can double the target: copies ≈ 2ⁿ after n cycles.
